title: SYNTHETIC: Effect of VL-9 on systolic blood pressure (RCT)

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text: This synthetic trial tests a fictional compound, VL-9. We randomized 120 fictional adults to VL-9 or placebo. Systolic blood pressure decreased by 11 mmHg in the treatment arm (p = 0.004). No serious adverse events were recorded.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text: Participants aged 40 to 65 with no prior cardiac disease were randomized 1:1 to VL-9 or placebo, as described in Fig. 1. Systolic blood pressure was measured at baseline and at week 16 by trained staff. Analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle, e.g. all randomized participants were included.

sections.name: Results
sections.text: Mean baseline systolic blood pressure was 129 mmHg in both arms. At week 16, systolic blood pressure decreased by 11 mmHg in the treatment arm relative to placebo (p = 0.004). Mild dizziness occurred in 10% of treated participants versus 2% on placebo.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: These synthetic findings suggest VL-9 may modify systolic blood pressure in this population. Longer follow-up is needed. Limitations include the single-region sample.

sections.name: References
sections.text: 1. Fictional A et al. Not a real paper. 2. Fictional B et al. Also not real.

title: SYNTHETIC: Effect of VL-9 on systolic blood pressure (cohort)

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text: In a fictional cohort of 800 adults, VL-9 users had lower systolic blood pressure than non-users (p = 0.02).

sections.name: Results
sections.text: Systolic blood pressure was 11 mmHg lower in users than non-users (p = 0.02). Estimates were similar across sexes. Adherence was self-reported, which limits interpretation.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: Residual confounding is possible. Differences in age range relative to trials may explain discordant findings.

title: SYNTHETIC: Effect of RT-450 on fasting glucose (cohort)

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text: In a fictional cohort of 1500 adults, RT-450 users showed no meaningful change in fasting glucose. Observational confounding cannot be excluded.

sections.name: Results
sections.text: Fasting glucose differed by 1 mg/dL between users and non-users (p = 0.34). Estimates were similar across sexes. Adherence was self-reported, which limits interpretation.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: Residual confounding is possible. Differences in age range relative to trials may explain discordant findings.
